accuracy.evidence: Coast as where land meets the sea and beach as the walkable shore checked against the KS1 geography key vocabulary (coast, beach, cliff, sea) and National Geographic Education 'Coast'; sandy beaches where waves deposit sand, rocky shores where waves erode hard rock, mudflats and salt marsh in sheltered estuaries (Field Studies Council shore guides); beach sand mostly weathered rock such as quartz plus shell fragments, formed over long periods (NOAA Ocean Service 'Where does sand come from?'); limpets clamp to rock, lugworms burrow in sand leaving casts, curlews probe mud with long curved bills, marram grass roots stabilise dunes, samphire grows on salt marsh (The Wildlife Trusts species pages).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets ideas young children hold about the seaside: every beach is sandy (lens prediction, m1, tag all); the edge of a pond or lake is a coast (lake decoy on the map, 'Tap the lake shore' button, m6, tag lake); sand grows or appears quickly (grind prediction, p5, tag grow; the grind message stresses a very long time); the same animals live on every coast (homes feedback, m3, tags home and bird); rock pools on any beach (tag pool).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcoast is built on coast-specific mechanics: a map whose wavy shoreline is traced segment by segment with a lake decoy, a draggable hand lens that zooms the sand, rock or mud texture under it, a wave dragged into a rock that breaks it from big rock to boulders to pebbles to sand, and coast panels that collect six named organisms and six clue cards. flagocean (what the ocean is) and flagseaneed (needs of sea animals) use none of these; the distinct gate measured at most a few percent overlap with any lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover before reading: tapping the lake gets 'fresh water inside the land', and only the traced shoreline counts; the three textures look and are named differently under the lens; each wave visibly breaks the rock into more, smaller pieces until only grains remain; a limpet dropped on sand is told it needs rock to clamp onto; clue counts end at 2 / 2 in each coast panel.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: 'the edge of any water, like a lake' / 'the middle of the sea' for what a coast is, 'yes, every beach is sand', and 'it grows on the sea floor' for where sand comes from. Each is tested by the task straight after, and the reveal line names the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions (what a coast is, are all beaches sandy, where rock pools are, where sand comes from, where a curlew feeds, what lives on rock, sinking boots). Wrong options carry tags lake, all, pool, grow, bird, home and clue, each with its own message naming the slip, e.g. 'Rock pools form in hollows between rocks when the sea goes out, so look on a rocky coast.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the kid and adult readability limits. Kid sentences are short and concrete ('A rocky coast has hard rocks and rock pools.'); coast, beach, sandy, rocky and muddy are shown on the canvas as well as named. Young-mode buttons are 56 px tall with larger text.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: what a coast is (and is not), three kinds, who lives on each, where sand comes from. Adult: curriculum link and key words, how each coast type forms, four named mistakes with the reason each organism needs its coast, then exactly what the lab does. No filler pattern matched and the 12% duplicate gate passed against 563 What Is the Ocean? and 643 What Ocean Animals Need.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android dark and light and iPhone 13 light screenshots after Show me. Fixed from the first pass: placed organisms were cramped 13 px labels over the textures, now each sits on its own pale tile with a 20 px emoji and its name, two per panel. The coastline, lake and labels sit above the feedback strip; the three coast strips and hand lens fit at 360 px.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin: 'Trace the next bit of coast' plus the lake and open-sea decoys, 'Look at coast 1/2/3', 'Send a wave', and one button per coast labelled with the current organism or clue. The canvas aria-label and live region carry each message, including the traced count. walk.cjs passed axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors; real pointer drags were tested for tracing, the lens and the wave.
